chunks.heading: What is a trigonometric identity?
chunks.body: An identity is a statement that is true for every value of the angle. It's different from an ordinary equation, which is usually only true for some values. sin^2(x) + cos^2(x) = 1 is an identity — it holds no matter what x is.

chunks.heading: The ratio identities
chunks.body: Two identities connect tan and cot to sin and cos: tan(θ) = sin(θ)/cos(θ), and cot(θ) = cos(θ)/sin(θ). This matches how [[mathadv-tangent-ratio|tan(A)]] was first defined as sin(A) divided by cos(A).

chunks.heading: The Pythagorean identity
chunks.body: sin^2(θ) + cos^2(θ) = 1 for every angle θ. It comes from Pythagoras' theorem applied to the circle definition of sine and cosine, where x^2 + y^2 = r^2.
chunks.checkText: sin^2(θ) + cos^2(θ) equals...

chunks.heading: Two more Pythagorean identities
chunks.body: Dividing [[mathadv-pythagorean-identity|sin^2(θ) + cos^2(θ) = 1]] by cos^2(θ) gives tan^2(θ) + 1 = sec^2(θ). Dividing it by sin^2(θ) instead gives cot^2(θ) + 1 = cosec^2(θ). Both come from the same starting identity.

chunks.heading: Complementary angle identities
chunks.body: Two angles are complementary if they add to 90°. For any angle θ, cos(90° − θ) = sin(θ). In the same way, cot(90° − θ) = tan(θ) and cosec(90° − θ) = sec(θ).

chunks.heading: How to prove an identity
chunks.body: To prove an identity, work on the left side (LHS) and the right side (RHS) separately, simplifying each using known identities, until they match. Never move a term from one side to the other like you would with an equation.

checkOptions.text: Simplify each side separately until they match
Move terms across the equals sign
Substitute a single value for the angle

chunks.heading: What is a trigonometric equation?
chunks.body: Unlike an [[mathadv-what-is-identity|identity]], a trigonometric equation like sin(x) = 0.5 is only true for particular values of x. Solving it means finding every value of x, within a given domain, that makes it true.

checkOptions.text: Every value of x that makes it true
A proof that it holds for all x

chunks.heading: Watch the domain
chunks.body: A [[mathadv-trig-equation|trigonometric equation]] is usually solved within a stated domain, like 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°. The domain controls how many solutions there are — a wider domain can give more solutions to the same equation.

chunks.heading: Solving trig equations: the quadrant method
chunks.body: To solve an equation like sin(x) = 0.5: find which quadrants give that sign using the [[mathadv-astc-rule|ASTC rule]], find the [[mathadv-related-acute-angle|related acute angle]], then mark the matching angles in those quadrants within the given domain.

checkOptions.text: Quadrants where the sign is correct

chunks.heading: Equations with reciprocal functions
chunks.body: To solve an equation with cosec, sec or cot, first take the reciprocal of both sides to rewrite it using sin, cos or tan instead. For example, sec(x) = 2 becomes cos(x) = 1/2.

chunks.heading: Solving equations with compound angles
chunks.body: For an equation like sin(2x) = 0.5, let u equal the compound angle (here, 2x). Rewrite the domain in terms of u, solve for u using the [[mathadv-quadrant-method-equations|quadrant method]], then convert back to find x.

chunks.heading: Turning two functions into one
chunks.body: Some equations mix two trigonometric functions, like sin(x) + sqrt(3)cos(x) = 0. Dividing every term by cos(x) turns it into an equation in tan(x) alone, which can then be solved.

chunks.heading: Naming a general triangle
chunks.body: In a general triangle ABC, each vertex has an uppercase letter, and each side is named with the lowercase version of the letter at the opposite vertex. So side a is opposite vertex A.
chunks.checkText: In triangle ABC, side b is the side opposite...

chunks.heading: The sine rule
chunks.body: In any [[mathadv-triangle-labeling-convention|triangle ABC]], a/sin(A) = b/sin(B) = c/sin(C). Each side's length divided by the sine of its opposite angle gives the same value for the whole triangle. Unlike the basic [[mathadv-sine-ratio|sine ratio]], this works for any triangle, not just right triangles.

chunks.heading: Using the sine rule to find a side
chunks.body: To find an unknown side with the [[mathadv-sine-rule|sine rule]], you need one side and two angles (AAS). Place the unknown side over the sine of its opposite angle, set it equal to the known side over the sine of its opposite angle, then solve.

checkOptions.text: Two sides and the angle between them

chunks.heading: The area formula for a triangle
chunks.body: In any [[mathadv-triangle-labeling-convention|triangle ABC]], area = (1/2) × b × c × sin(A), using two sides and the angle between them. It generalises the familiar area = (1/2) × base × height formula.

chunks.heading: Finding a side or angle from the area
chunks.body: If you know a triangle's area along with two sides or two angles, you can rearrange the [[mathadv-area-formula|area formula]] to find the missing side or angle.

chunks.heading: The ambiguous case: two triangles from one set of data
chunks.body: When you know two sides and a non-included angle (ASS), using the [[mathadv-sine-rule|sine rule]] to find another angle can give two possible answers: one acute, one obtuse. Both may form a valid triangle, so check the angle sum to see if each is possible.

chunks.heading: The cosine rule
chunks.body: In any [[mathadv-triangle-labeling-convention|triangle ABC]], a^2 = b^2 + c^2 − 2bc·cos(A). It relates the square of one side to the squares of the other two sides and the cosine of the angle between them.

chunks.heading: The cosine rule and Pythagoras' theorem
chunks.body: When angle A is 90°, cos(A) = 0, so the [[mathadv-cosine-rule|cosine rule]] simplifies to a^2 = b^2 + c^2 — exactly Pythagoras' theorem. The cosine rule is really a generalisation of Pythagoras' theorem to any triangle.

chunks.heading: Using the cosine rule to find a side
chunks.body: To find an unknown side with the [[mathadv-cosine-rule|cosine rule]], you need two sides and the angle between them (SAS). Substitute these into the formula and solve for the unknown side.

checkOptions.text: Two sides and the angle between them

chunks.heading: Using the cosine rule to find an angle
chunks.body: If all three sides of a triangle are known (SSS), rearrange the [[mathadv-cosine-rule|cosine rule]] to solve for the cosine of an angle. Unlike the sine rule, this always gives exactly one answer for the angle.

chunks.heading: Choosing the right rule
chunks.body: Which rule to use depends on what's known. Two angles and a side (AAS) needs the [[mathadv-sine-rule|sine rule]]. Two sides and the angle between them (SAS) needs the [[mathadv-cosine-rule|cosine rule]]. All three sides (SSS) also needs the cosine rule, but to find an angle instead.

chunks.heading: Two-step triangle problems
chunks.body: Some triangle problems need two steps: first find a missing side or angle using [[mathadv-choosing-the-rule|the right rule]], then use that new information with another rule to find what's actually being asked for.

checkOptions.text: Finding one unknown, then using it to find another
Using the same formula twice on the same value

chunks.heading: Amplitude of a wave
chunks.body: The amplitude of a wave is how far it rises above (or falls below) its middle value. Both y = sin(x) and y = cos(x) have a maximum of 1, a minimum of −1, and a middle value of 0, so both have amplitude 1.

chunks.heading: The period of a trig graph
chunks.body: The period of a repeating graph is the length of its smallest repeating pattern. y = sin(x) and y = cos(x) repeat every [[mathadv-full-turn-radians|full revolution]], so they have period 2π. y = tan(x) repeats twice as often, with period π.

chunks.heading: Odd and even functions
chunks.body: A function is odd if f(−x) = −f(x); its graph has point symmetry about the origin. sin(x) and tan(x) are odd. A function is even if f(−x) = f(x); its graph has line symmetry in the y-axis. cos(x) is even.
